description: Brain development from brain stem to cortex, and the roles of nature and nurture.
content_html:
The Developing Brain

You started life as a single cell. Within weeks of conception, a simple tube of neural tissue had formed, and from this beginning every thought you have ever had, every skill you have ever learned, grew. Understanding how the brain builds itself — and what shapes that process — sits at the heart of developmental psychology.

Brain development follows a pattern that moves from the simplest, most essential structures through to the most complex. The brain does not switch on all at once; it assembles itself in layers, with the parts that keep you alive forming first and the parts that allow you to think, reason and create developing last. This ordering is not random — it reflects millions of years of evolution prioritising survival over sophisticated cognition.

Simple Neural Structures in the Womb

In the first weeks after conception the embryo develops a neural tube. This structure closes and begins to swell at one end, forming the basic regions of the brain. By the time a baby is born, these regions have become far more elaborate, but their foundations were laid before the second trimester had even begun.

The brain develops from the bottom upwards and from the inside outwards. The innermost, oldest structures form first; the outer, newer structures form last. Psychologists describe four key regions in the order they typically mature: the brain stem, the thalamus, the cerebellum, and the cortex.

Key Fact

Brain development follows a bottom-up sequence: brain stem (autonomic functions), thalamus (sensory processing), cerebellum (movement coordination) and cortex (higher cognition). Each layer builds on the one below it.

The Brain Stem: Keeping Alive

The brain stem is the most primitive structure, and it develops first. It controls autonomic functions — the processes that keep you alive without you having to think about them. Breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, swallowing and the sleep–wake cycle are all regulated here. A newborn baby’s brain stem is functional from birth, which is why they breathe, cry and sleep even though the rest of their brain is still immature.

The Thalamus: Routing Sensory Information

Above the brain stem sits the thalamus. It matures next and acts as the brain’s central switchboard for sensory processing. Almost all sensory signals — from your eyes, ears, skin and tongue — are routed through the thalamus before reaching the cortex for interpretation. Without a functioning thalamus, even a fully developed cortex could not receive the information it needs to make sense of the world.

This is why newborns respond quickly to touch, sound and light even before they can make sense of what they are experiencing. The thalamus is relaying the signals; it is the cortex — still developing — that will eventually interpret them fully.

The cerebellum sits at the back of the brain below the cortex. It is responsible for coordinating movement and balance. When a child learns to walk, the cerebellum is doing the heavy lifting — gradually building a smooth, coordinated programme of movement from what was initially a stumbling series of adjustments. The cerebellum also plays a role in procedural skills: riding a bike, typing and catching a ball all rely on cerebellar coordination.

The cerebellum continues to develop into early childhood, which is why babies cannot walk immediately after birth. Even in adulthood, damage to the cerebellum causes difficulties with balance and coordination rather than with thinking or memory — confirming how precisely localised its function is.

The Cortex: Thinking and Cognition

The outermost layer of the brain is the cortex. It is the last structure to develop and the one that develops for the longest time — the prefrontal cortex, which handles planning and decision-making, does not fully mature until a person’s mid-twenties. The cortex is responsible for higher-order cognition: language, abstract thinking, problem-solving, creativity and conscious perception.

Because the cortex develops so late and over such a long period, it is the part of the brain most shaped by experience after birth. This has important implications for education: the brain is not a finished product at birth but a work in progress that continues to be built by the experiences a child has.

Key Fact

The cortex is responsible for higher cognition — language, reasoning and problem-solving — and is the last region to mature. Its prolonged development means it is the part of the brain most open to being shaped by learning and experience after birth.

The debate about nature versus nurture asks how much of our development is determined by our genes (nature) and how much by our environment and experiences (nurture). In brain development, both play essential roles.

The nature side of the argument points to the fact that the basic sequence of brain development — brain stem first, cortex last — is the same in all humans. Genes direct the initial construction: which neurons form, how they connect and what functions they serve. This blueprint is inherited.

The nurture side points to the fact that the brain is not a static structure. Neurons that are stimulated by experience form stronger connections (synapses), while those that are not used weaken or disappear — a process called synaptic pruning. Language development offers a clear example: babies are born with the capacity to learn any language, but they will only acquire the specific language(s) they hear around them. The environment shapes which neural pathways are strengthened.

Most psychologists today accept that brain development is an interaction of both nature and nurture. Genes set the parameters; experience fills in the detail. Neither alone can fully explain how the human brain becomes what it is.
exam_tip_html: For ‘Describe’ questions on brain development, work through the four structures in order: brain stem, thalamus, cerebellum, cortex. Name each structure, state what it does, and note when it matures relative to the others — this gives you a clear three-mark answer. For ‘Explain’ questions on nature and nurture in development, avoid saying one is more important than the other without justifying it — the strongest answers acknowledge the interaction.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The brain develops in a bottom-up sequence: brain stem (autonomic functions), thalamus (sensory relay), cerebellum (movement) and cortex (cognition). This sequence is genetically determined.
  • The cortex is the last structure to mature and the most influenced by experience, which is why learning and environment shape higher cognitive development well into adulthood.
  • Brain development reflects both nature (genetic blueprint for structure and sequence) and nurture (experience strengthens or prunes neural connections); neither alone is sufficient.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following brain structures develops first?
A) Cortex
B) Cerebellum
C) Brain stem
D) Thalamus
Define what is meant by 'autonomic functions'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear definition identifying (1) processes that happen automatically/without conscious thought, AND (2) a correct example such as breathing, heartbeat or digestion — e.g. 'Body processes that operate without conscious control, such as breathing and heart rate.' [2 marks].
Secure: Correct core idea but vague or missing example [1 mark].
Developing: Partial reference to automatic processes but imprecise [0–1 mark].
Emerging: Incorrect or very vague [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the thalamus in brain development.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- The thalamus acts as a relay station for sensory information.
- It routes signals from the senses (sight, hearing, touch, etc.) to the correct area of the cortex.
- It develops after the brain stem but before the cerebellum and cortex.
- Newborns can respond to sensory stimuli partly because the thalamus is functional at birth.
Mastering: All three elements (function, timing, implication) clearly stated.
Secure: Two elements, terminology correct.
Developing: One element with some accuracy.
Emerging: Limited or vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain how both nature and nurture contribute to early brain development.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Nature: genes direct the basic sequence and structure of brain development (brain stem → thalamus → cerebellum → cortex) — this sequence is universal and not influenced by environment.
- Nurture: experience after birth shapes which neural connections are strengthened or pruned — e.g. language acquisition shows how stimulation develops specific pathways.
- Interaction point: genes set the initial blueprint but environment determines which parts of that blueprint are fully developed.
Mastering: Both nature and nurture clearly explained with developed examples and interaction noted.
Secure: Both explained but interaction not elaborated.
Developing: One side explained well, other only mentioned.
Emerging: Vague reference to nature and nurture without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe the sequence of brain development from simple neural structures in the womb through to the cortex.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should cover:
- Starting point: neural tube forms in early embryonic development.
- Brain stem develops first: controls autonomic functions (breathing, heart rate, sleep).
- Thalamus develops next: acts as a relay for sensory processing.
- Cerebellum develops: coordinates movement and balance, continues maturing into early childhood.
- Cortex develops last: responsible for higher cognition (language, reasoning, planning); continues maturing into the mid-twenties.
Mastering: All five stages described accurately and in correct order.
Secure: Four stages described correctly.
Developing: Three stages with some inaccuracy.
Emerging: One or two stages, limited accuracy.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the roles of nature and nurture in early brain development.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1):
- Nature: the genetic blueprint determines the sequence (brain stem → thalamus → cerebellum → cortex) and the basic architecture of the brain. This is universal across humans.
- Nurture: experience shapes neural connections through synaptic strengthening and pruning. The cortex is particularly open to environmental influence due to its prolonged development.
- Example: language acquisition — babies can learn any language but acquire only those they are exposed to.

Evaluation (AO3):
- Strength of nature view: the consistency of developmental sequence across all humans regardless of culture or environment supports a strong genetic component.
- Limitation of nature-only view: identical twins do not always develop identically, suggesting environment plays a role even when genes are the same.
- Strength of nurture view: studies of children raised in deprived environments (e.g. limited stimulation) show reduced cortical development, showing experience matters.
- Limitation of nurture-only view: basic brain structures form even in the absence of stimulation, suggesting nature sets the foundation that nurture cannot override.
- Interactionist conclusion: most psychologists see development as an interaction; genes provide the scaffold, experience determines what is built on it.

Mastering: Accurate, detailed description of both roles with clear, elaborated evaluation including interaction.
Secure: Both described with some evaluation and elaboration.
Developing: Description present; evaluation brief or one-sided.
Emerging: Basic description, little evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which part of the brain is responsible for controlling autonomic functions such as breathing and heart rate?
Which brain structure acts as a relay station, routing sensory information to the correct area of the cortex?
The _____ is the last brain structure to develop and is responsible for higher cognitive functions such as reasoning and language.
The nature side of the nature–nurture debate focuses on the role of _____ inheritance in shaping development.
Match each brain structure to its main function:
right: Routes sensory signals to the cortex
Controls breathing, heart rate and sleep

flashcard_questions.q: What is the first brain structure to develop in the womb?
flashcard_questions.a: The brain stem, which controls autonomic functions like breathing and heartbeat.

flashcard_questions.q: What function does the brain stem control?
flashcard_questions.a: Automatic functions such as breathing, heart rate and the sleep–wake cycle.

flashcard_questions.q: What role does the thalamus play in the developing brain?
flashcard_questions.a: It acts as a relay station, routing sensory information to the correct area of the cortex.

flashcard_questions.q: Which brain structure coordinates movement, balance and fine motor skills?
Which brain structure is responsible for reasoning, language and problem-solving?
In what order do the four key brain regions typically develop?
Why does the prolonged development of the cortex matter for education?
flashcard_questions.a: Because it remains open to being shaped by learning and experience well into adulthood.

flashcard_questions.q: What early structure in the embryo later becomes the brain and spinal cord?
In the nature–nurture debate, what does the 'nature' side argue shapes brain development?
flashcard_questions.a: Genetic inheritance — genes direct the basic sequence and structure of the brain.

flashcard_questions.q: In the nature–nurture debate, what does the 'nurture' side argue shapes brain development?
flashcard_questions.a: Experience after birth strengthens or prunes neural connections.
The process by which unused neural connections weaken and disappear, shaped by experience.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do newborns respond to sound and touch even though their cortex is immature?
flashcard_questions.a: Because the thalamus is already functional and relays sensory signals at birth.

glossary_terms.definition: A hollow tube of cells that forms in early embryonic development and later differentiates into the brain and spinal cord.
The oldest part of the brain, connecting it to the spinal cord and controlling vital automatic functions such as breathing, heart rate and sleeping.
Body processes that happen automatically and without conscious control, such as breathing, heartbeat and digestion.
A structure in the middle of the brain that acts as a relay station, routing sensory information from the body to the correct part of the cortex.
The processing of information from the senses — sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell.
A structure at the back and base of the brain responsible for coordinating movement, balance and fine motor skills.
The wrinkled outer layer of the brain responsible for higher-level functions such as reasoning, language, planning, memory and conscious thought.
The role that genetic inheritance and biological factors play in shaping development.
The role that environment, experiences and learning play in shaping development.
